title: Passing the NREMT
summary: How the computer-adaptive exam actually works, how to read the questions, the topics people fail on, the skill stations, New Jersey certification, and a four-week plan that works.

lessons.title: How the cognitive exam actually works
lessons.body:
The National Registry cognitive exam is not a normal test. Understanding the machine removes most of the fear, because the thing that terrifies people about it is a design feature, not a sign of failure.

## Computer-adaptive testing

The exam is a **computer-adaptive test (CAT)**. It starts with a question of moderate difficulty. Get it right and the next one is harder; get it wrong and the next one is easier. The computer is not counting your score — it is estimating your ability and narrowing the estimate with every answer.

The exam ends when the computer is `95%` confident that your ability is either above or below the passing standard, or when you hit the question limit or the clock.

- **Length:** minimum `70` questions, maximum `120`.
- **Time:** `2 hours` total, including any break you take.
- Some items are unscored pilot questions being tested for future exams. You cannot tell which.

> **Key:** Because the computer keeps feeding you questions at the edge of your ability, a passing candidate feels like they are guessing about half the time. Feeling terrible during the exam is the normal experience of passing. Do not let it change how you answer.

The exam can shut off at `70` questions for someone who is clearly passing or clearly failing. It is not true that shutting off early is good or bad news — it means the computer got confident, in one direction or the other.

## The five content domains

The National Registry rebuilt the EMT test plan on `April 7, 2025`. The old clinical domains — airway, cardiology, trauma, medical and OB — are gone. The exam is now organized around the steps of patient assessment, and items from every clinical area are spread across those steps.

| Domain | Share of the exam |
|---|---|
| Scene Size-Up and Safety | `15 to 19%` |
| Primary Assessment | `39 to 43%` |
| Secondary Assessment | `5 to 9%` |
| Patient Treatment and Transport | `20 to 24%` |
| Operations | `10 to 14%` |

Pediatric items are integrated throughout the content rather than held to a fixed share.

Read that table once more. **Primary Assessment alone is roughly `40%` of the exam** — finding and fixing life threats in the right order. That is why this module spends so much time on the priority sequence: it is not a study trick, it is the largest thing the test measures.

## Passing, results and retesting

There is no percentage score and no curve. You pass by demonstrating, with `95%` confidence, entry-level competence at the standard. The result is pass or fail, with no number attached.

- **Results** post to your National Registry account, usually within `1 to 2 business days`.
- **Failed attempt:** you must wait `15 days` before retesting, and you get a report showing which domains were below standard.
- **After three failed attempts:** you must complete a documented remedial training program before you are allowed three more attempts, for a maximum of `6` total. After that, the entire course must be repeated.

> **On the exam:** The report after a failure is the most useful study guide you will ever get, because it names the domains you were below standard in. Study those, not the ones you enjoy.

## Getting in the door

You apply through the National Registry website after your course director verifies your course completion. You pay the exam fee — roughly `$104` for the EMT cognitive exam, so check the current amount — and receive an **Authorization to Test (ATT)** letter. That letter contains your eligibility window and lets you schedule at a **Pearson VUE** testing center. Do not schedule for a day you are working a shift.
keyPoints: The exam is computer-adaptive: 70 to 120 questions in 2 hours, ending when the computer is 95% confident about your ability.
Feeling like you are failing throughout is the normal experience of a passing candidate.
Primary Assessment is the biggest domain at 39 to 43%; Scene Size-Up and Safety is 15 to 19%.
Pediatric items are integrated throughout the exam rather than fixed at a set percentage.
Results in 1 to 2 business days; 15-day wait to retest; three attempts, then remediation, six total.

checks.q: Your exam shuts off at 70 questions. What does that tell you?
choices: You definitely passed
You definitely failed
The computer reached 95% confidence in one direction, which could be either pass or fail
The computer malfunctioned and the exam must be retaken
checks.why: An early stop means the algorithm became confident about your ability relative to the standard. It says nothing about which direction, so drawing conclusions from question count is pointless.

checks.q: Which content domain makes up the largest share of the EMT cognitive exam?
choices: Scene Size-Up and Safety
Primary Assessment
Operations
Secondary Assessment
checks.why: Under the test plan that took effect April 7, 2025, Primary Assessment is 39 to 43% of the exam, close to half. Scene Size-Up and Safety is 15 to 19%, Operations 10 to 14%, and Secondary Assessment is the smallest at 5 to 9%.

checks.q: How long must you wait after a failed attempt before retesting, and how many attempts do you get before remediation is required?
choices: 15 days; three attempts
24 hours; unlimited attempts
30 days; two attempts
90 days; six attempts
checks.why: The mandatory wait is 15 days between attempts, and after three failures you must complete a documented remedial program before three more attempts, six in total.

lessons.title: How to read an NREMT question
lessons.body:
Most people who fail this exam know the medicine. They lose to the question format. Every item is built the same way, and once you can see the frame, half the wrong answers eliminate themselves.

## The anatomy of an item

A **stem** presents a scenario and asks one question. Four **choices** follow: one correct answer, and three **distractors** that are wrong for specific, designed reasons. There is no 'all of the above,' no trick wording, and no partial credit. Exactly one choice is the single best answer.

Distractors usually come in recognizable flavors: something correct but done at the wrong time, something that treats a different problem, something outside your scope, and something that sounds authoritative but is harmful.

## Cue words decide the answer

Read the last line of the stem twice. These words change which choice is right, even when several choices are things you would actually do.

| Cue word | What it is asking |
|---|---|
| **first**, **initial**, **immediately** | What comes earliest in the sequence, right now |
| **next** | Assume everything before it is done; what follows |
| **best**, **most appropriate** | Several are acceptable — pick the highest standard of care |
| **priority** | Ranked by threat to life |
| **should you suspect** | Pattern recognition, not treatment |
| **except**, **least likely** | The one that does not belong; read very slowly |

> **Trap:** The most common error is picking a treatment when the stem asked what you do **first** and you have not yet assessed. If the patient's airway status is unknown, assessing the airway beats treating anything.

## When assess beats treat

If the stem has not told you an airway is open, breathing is adequate, and circulation is intact, the answer is usually to find that out. Treatment answers become correct once the stem has already handed you the assessment findings.

## When transport is the answer

Choose transport when the problem cannot be fixed in the field: internal bleeding, a prolapsed cord, an ectopic pregnancy, a limb presentation, an epidural bleed, a patient needing surgery. If a choice is 'perform a definitive intervention on scene' and no EMT skill can do it, transport wins.

## When calling ALS is the answer

Call ALS when the patient needs a drug or a skill above your level and time permits: an unmanageable airway, cardiac arrest, seizures that will not stop, IV dextrose for an unresponsive hypoglycemic patient, severe respiratory distress. Requesting ALS is almost never the **first** action, though — it comes after the immediate life threat is addressed. If a choice says 'call ALS' and the patient is not breathing, ventilating comes first.

## The assumptions you are supposed to make

The National Registry writes to a national standard of care, not to any local protocol. Unless a stem says otherwise, assume:

- You have a **partner** and a full BLS ambulance with complete equipment.
- The scene is safe unless the stem raises a hazard.
- You have **standing orders** for everything in the standard EMT scope.
- You follow the **national standard**, not what your instructor says your county does.

> **On the exam:** 'All patients get high-flow oxygen' has not been correct for years. Oxygen is titrated to `94 to 98%`, or `88 to 92%` in COPD. A choice offering a nonrebreather to an alert patient with a normal saturation is a distractor.

## Working an item

1. Read the stem once for the story, then read the last line again for the cue word.
2. Predict your answer before you look at the choices.
3. Eliminate anything outside EMT scope, anything harmful, and anything that treats the wrong problem.
4. Of the remaining, pick the one that comes first in the priority sequence.
5. Answer and move on. You cannot go back, and you cannot flag items on an adaptive exam.
keyPoints: Cue words decide the answer: first, next, best, most appropriate, priority, except.
If assessment findings are missing from the stem, assess before you treat.
Transport is the answer when no EMT skill can fix the problem; ALS is the answer when a higher-level drug or skill is needed, but rarely as the first action.
Assume a partner, a fully stocked BLS unit, standing orders, and the national standard of care.
Predict the answer before reading the choices, then eliminate scope violations and harmful options.

checks.q: A stem ends with 'Which of the following should you do FIRST?' Two of the four choices are things you would eventually do. How do you choose?
choices: Pick the more advanced intervention
Pick whichever comes earliest in the assessment and priority sequence
Pick the one that takes the least time
Pick the one your local protocol lists first
checks.why: 'First' asks about sequence, not about which action is most impressive. The national priority order decides it, and local protocol is explicitly not the standard the exam uses.

checks.q: Which assumption is correct when answering an NREMT item?
choices: You are alone with a jump bag and no ambulance
You must call medical control before every intervention
You have a partner, a fully equipped BLS ambulance, and standing orders for the EMT scope
You should answer based on your county's protocol
checks.why: The exam is written to the national standard with a fully resourced BLS response. Answering from local protocol variation is one of the most common ways experienced students lose points.

lessons.title: The unbreakable priority order
lessons.body:
Almost every 'what do you do first' item is answered by one ordered list. Learn it as a reflex and you will answer correctly even on material you do not know well.

## The order

1. **Scene safety.** If there is any hazard in the stem — downed wires, fire, a weapon, an aggressive bystander, a running engine, an unstable vehicle — nothing else happens until it is addressed. On the exam this often means 'stage until police secure the scene.' Answers that have you approaching an unsecured scene are always wrong.
2. **Standard precautions (BSI).** Gloves at minimum, eye protection for anything spraying, a mask for airborne concerns. If a choice is 'apply personal protective equipment' and you have not yet touched the patient, it outranks care.
3. **General impression and level of consciousness.** Sick or not sick, and AVPU.
4. **Airway.** Open it, keep it open, suction it.
5. **Breathing.** Adequate rate and depth. Inadequate breathing means ventilate — not oxygen by mask, ventilate.
6. **Circulation.** Pulse, major bleeding, skin signs, perfusion.
7. **Disability and exposure.** Neuro status, then find the injuries.
8. **Everything else:** history, vitals, secondary assessment, splinting, comfort.

> **Key:** Assess and correct life threats in the primary survey before you take a history or a full set of vitals. A choice offering 'obtain a SAMPLE history' while the patient has a compromised airway is always wrong.

## The two exceptions worth knowing

**Massive external hemorrhage comes before airway.** If the patient is spurting blood from an extremity, a tourniquet goes on before you open the airway. Bleeding that fast empties the tank in minutes. This is the X in the XABC sequence.

**In cardiac arrest, compressions come first.** Adult arrest is CAB, not ABC: start compressions, then airway, then breathing. That is because the blood in an adult who just arrested is still oxygenated and the problem is that nothing is moving it. Newborns are the opposite — their arrest is a breathing problem, so ventilation leads.

## Ventilate versus oxygenate

This single distinction decides a large number of airway items.

| Finding | Action |
|---|---|
| Breathing adequately, saturation low | Oxygen by cannula or nonrebreather, titrated |
| Breathing **inadequately** (too slow, too shallow, agonal) | **Assist ventilations with a BVM** |
| Not breathing at all, has a pulse | BVM at `1 breath every 6 seconds` for adults, `1 every 2 to 3 seconds` for children |
| No breathing, no pulse | Compressions first, then ventilation, AED as soon as available |

> **Trap:** A respiratory rate of `28` with shallow, barely-moving chest is inadequate breathing. The fast number tempts people to call it adequate. Depth matters as much as rate, and the correct action is assisted ventilation.

## Treat what you find, when you find it

The primary survey is not a list you complete and then go back to. You fix each problem as you find it. Found an obstructed airway at step 4? Fix it before you check breathing. That is why 'continue the assessment' is rarely the right answer when the stem just handed you a life threat.

## Scene size-up items

Scene size-up is scene safety, standard precautions, mechanism of injury or nature of illness, number of patients, and the need for additional resources. Calling for more ambulances happens during size-up, before you are committed to one patient — once you are kneeling next to patient one, nobody is counting the rest.
keyPoints: Scene safety, then BSI, then general impression, then airway, breathing, circulation, then everything else.
Massive external hemorrhage is treated before the airway; in adult cardiac arrest compressions come before airway.
Inadequate breathing means assist ventilations with a BVM, not apply a nonrebreather.
Fix each life threat as you find it rather than finishing the survey first.
Count patients and call for resources during scene size-up, before committing to one patient.

checks.q: A patient is found with agonal gasps at about 6 per minute and a weak carotid pulse. What is the correct action?
choices: Apply a nonrebreather at 15 L/min
Begin chest compressions
Assist ventilations with a bag-valve mask
Obtain a full set of vital signs
checks.why: Agonal gasps are inadequate breathing, and a mask only delivers oxygen to someone who is moving air. With a pulse present, compressions are not indicated, and vitals wait until the life threat is managed.

checks.q: You find a patient with arterial bleeding from a thigh laceration and noisy breathing. What do you do first?
choices: Control the hemorrhage with a tourniquet
Open the airway with a jaw thrust
Apply oxygen
Take a blood pressure
checks.why: Massive external hemorrhage precedes airway in the XABC sequence because arterial bleeding can empty the vascular space in minutes. The airway is addressed immediately afterward.

checks.q: Arriving at a shooting scene, you see the patient on the sidewalk and a man shouting nearby. Police have not arrived. What is your action?
choices: Approach quickly and drag the patient to the ambulance
Stage at a safe distance until law enforcement secures the scene
Ask the shouting man to step back and then begin care
Begin care from behind the ambulance
checks.why: Scene safety outranks everything, and an unsecured violent scene is not entered. A rescuer who becomes a second patient helps nobody, and this is one of the few absolutes on the exam.

lessons.title: Most-missed topics: airway, oxygen and resuscitation
lessons.body:
These numbers appear on almost every exam, and they are pure recall. There is no reasoning shortcut — you either have them or you guess.

## Airway maneuvers and adjuncts

- **Head-tilt chin-lift** for a patient with no suspected spinal injury. **Jaw thrust** when spinal injury is suspected.
- **Oropharyngeal airway (OPA):** only for a patient with **no gag reflex**. Size from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe or angle of the jaw. In adults, insert upside down and rotate `180 degrees`; in children, insert right side up with a tongue depressor.
- **Nasopharyngeal airway (NPA):** tolerated by patients with a gag reflex. Size from the nostril to the earlobe. Lubricate, bevel toward the septum, insert straight back along the floor of the nose, not upward. Avoid with suspected skull fracture or facial trauma.
- **Suction:** rigid catheter for the mouth, never pushed past the base of the tongue. Suction on the way out, for no more than `10 to 15 seconds` in an adult, `10 seconds` in a child, `5 seconds` in an infant. Always suction before ventilating a patient with fluid in the airway.

## Oxygen numbers

| Device | Flow | Delivered |
|---|---|---|
| Nasal cannula | `1 to 6 L/min` | `24 to 44%` |
| Simple mask | `6 to 10 L/min` | `35 to 60%` |
| Nonrebreather | `10 to 15 L/min` | `80 to 90%`+ |
| BVM with reservoir | `15 L/min` | near `100%` |

Target saturation is `94 to 98%`, or `88 to 92%` for COPD. In suspected carbon monoxide poisoning, ignore the pulse oximeter and use `15 L/min` by nonrebreather.

## CPR numbers

| | Adult | Child (1 year to puberty) | Infant (under 1 year) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Compression rate | `100 to 120/min` | `100 to 120/min` | `100 to 120/min` |
| Depth | At least `2 inches`, not over `2.4` | About `2 inches`, one third of chest | About `1.5 inches`, one third of chest |
| Ratio, one rescuer | `30:2` | `30:2` | `30:2` |
| Ratio, two rescuers | `30:2` | `15:2` | `15:2` |
| Technique | Two hands, lower half of sternum | One or two hands | Two fingers, or two thumbs with two rescuers |

With an advanced airway in place, compressions are continuous and ventilation is `1 breath every 6 seconds` for adults. Newborn resuscitation is the exception to everything above: `3:1` at `120 events per minute`.

Switch compressors every `2 minutes`, allow full chest recoil, and keep interruptions under `10 seconds`.

> **Key:** Attach the AED as soon as it arrives and follow its prompts. Resume compressions **immediately** after a shock without checking a pulse. Do not shock a patient in water or on a metal surface, do not place pads over a pacemaker bulge or a medication patch, and dry a wet chest first.

## Cardiac recognition

Acute coronary syndrome can present without chest pain, especially in women, older adults and diabetics — instead you get shortness of breath, nausea, fatigue, or discomfort in the jaw, back or arm.

Left-sided heart failure backs fluid into the lungs: crackles, pink frothy sputum, orthopnea. Right-sided failure backs fluid into the body: swollen ankles, distended neck veins, enlarged liver.

Aspirin is `324 mg` chewed. Nitroglycerin is `0.4 mg` sublingual, up to `3 doses`, `5 minutes` apart, with a systolic above `100` and no PDE-5 inhibitor in `24 to 48 hours`.

> **On the exam:** A stroke item wants the same three things every time: identify the deficit with a stroke scale, establish the **last known well** time, and transport to a stroke center with early notification. Do not give aspirin for a stroke.
keyPoints: OPA needs no gag reflex; NPA is tolerated with one but is avoided in suspected skull fracture.
Suction on the way out: 10 to 15 seconds adult, 10 child, 5 infant.
CPR is 100 to 120 per minute, at least 2 inches in adults, 30:2 single rescuer and 15:2 for two-rescuer child and infant.
Resume compressions immediately after an AED shock without a pulse check, and switch compressors every 2 minutes.
Stroke items want a stroke scale, a last-known-well time, and a stroke center — never aspirin.

checks.q: Two rescuers are performing CPR on an 8-month-old. What compression-to-ventilation ratio should they use?
checks.why: Two-rescuer child and infant CPR is 15:2; single-rescuer is 30:2. The 3:1 ratio belongs to newborn resuscitation immediately after birth, not to an 8-month-old.

checks.q: An unresponsive patient vomits. You have suction ready. How long may you suction an adult at one time?
choices: No more than 5 seconds
No more than 30 seconds
No more than 10 to 15 seconds
Until the airway is completely clear, regardless of time
checks.why: Suctioning removes oxygen along with fluid, so adult suction is limited to 10 to 15 seconds, 10 for a child and 5 for an infant, then reoxygenate before repeating.

checks.q: The AED delivers a shock. What is the immediate next action?
choices: Check for a pulse for 10 seconds
Analyze the rhythm again
Resume chest compressions immediately
Give two rescue breaths
checks.why: Compressions resume right away because a heart that has just converted still needs perfusion, and pulse checks waste the seconds that matter. The next analysis comes after 2 minutes of CPR.

lessons.title: Most-missed topics: pediatrics, OB, shock and medications
lessons.body:
The largest domain on the exam is medical and OB-GYN. This lesson is the compressed version of the content that shows up most.

## Pediatric vitals and airway

| Age | Respirations | Heart rate | Systolic BP |
|---|---|---|---|
| Newborn | 30-60 | 100-180 | 60-90 |
| Infant | 25-50 | 100-160 | 70-95 |
| Toddler | 20-30 | 90-150 | 80-100 |
| Preschool | 20-28 | 80-140 | 80-100 |
| School age | 18-25 | 70-120 | 80-110 |
| Adolescent | 12-20 | 60-100 | 90-110 |

Minimum acceptable systolic for ages `1 to 10` is `70 plus twice the age in years`.

Children have big heads, big tongues and soft tracheas: keep the head **neutral** in infants, pad under the shoulders, never hyperextend. Ventilate at `1 breath every 2 to 3 seconds`. **Bradycardia in a child means hypoxia** until proven otherwise, and the treatment is ventilation.

The **pediatric assessment triangle** is appearance, work of breathing, and circulation to skin, formed from the doorway before you touch the child.

## OB in one page

- **Imminent delivery:** crowning, urge to push, contractions `2 to 3 minutes` apart lasting `60 to 90 seconds`. Crowning means deliver on scene.
- **Left lateral tilt** after `20 weeks` for any supine pregnant patient.
- **Previa** is painless bright red bleeding; **abruption** is painful dark bleeding with a rigid uterus.
- **Preeclampsia** is BP `140/90` or higher after `20 weeks` with headache, vision changes and edema. A seizure makes it eclampsia: left lateral, protect, dim and quiet, transport.
- **Prolapsed cord:** knee-chest or Trendelenburg, gloved hand lifts the presenting part off the cord and stays there, moist dressing, immediate transport.
- **Newborn:** warm, dry, stimulate, position. Ventilate at `40 to 60/min` if apneic or heart rate under `100`. Compressions `3:1` if the rate stays under `60` after `30 seconds` of good ventilation. APGAR at `1` and `5` minutes, `7 to 10` normal.

## Shock

Shock is inadequate tissue perfusion. The body compensates by squeezing vessels and speeding the heart, which is why **blood pressure falls last**.

| Type | Mechanism | Distinguishing sign |
|---|---|---|
| Hypovolemic | Lost volume | Cool, pale, clammy; tachycardia |
| Cardiogenic | Pump failure | Crackles, distended neck veins, history of MI |
| Distributive (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic) | Vessels dilate | Warm or flushed skin; neurogenic gives **slow** heart rate with warm dry skin below the injury |
| Obstructive | Flow blocked | Tension pneumothorax with tracheal shift, or tamponade with muffled tones |

Compensated shock has a normal blood pressure with tachycardia, anxiety and delayed capillary refill. Decompensated shock has a falling pressure and altered mental status. Treatment is oxygen, bleeding control, supine position, warmth, and rapid transport.

> **Trap:** Neurogenic shock is the one that breaks the pattern — hypotension with **bradycardia** and warm, dry, flushed skin, because the injured spinal cord cannot tell the vessels to constrict or the heart to speed up.

## Medication contraindications

These exact pairings are tested constantly.

- **Aspirin:** not with active GI bleeding, a bleeding stroke, an allergy, or a child with fever.
- **Nitroglycerin:** not with a systolic under `100`, a PDE-5 inhibitor within `24 hours` (sildenafil, vardenafil) or `48 hours` (tadalafil), a head injury, or after `3` doses.
- **Oral glucose:** not without a gag reflex or the ability to swallow.
- **Activated charcoal:** not for caustics, alcohols, metals or hydrocarbons, and not without an intact gag reflex.
- **Epinephrine:** no absolute contraindication in true anaphylaxis. `0.3 mg` adult, `0.15 mg` for `15 to 30 kg`.
- **Naloxone:** ventilate first, titrate to breathing, expect re-sedation in `30 to 90 minutes`.

> **Key:** When a question offers a medication, check the contraindication list before you check whether it fits the complaint. The exam loves a patient whose symptoms are perfect for a drug he must not receive.
keyPoints: Minimum systolic for children 1 to 10 is 70 plus twice the age; bradycardia in a child means hypoxia.
Crowning means deliver on scene; left lateral tilt for any supine pregnant patient past 20 weeks.
Newborn: ventilate at 40 to 60 if apneic or heart rate under 100; compressions 3:1 under 60 after 30 seconds.
Blood pressure falls last in shock; neurogenic shock is the exception with bradycardia and warm dry skin.
Check contraindications before indications — the exam builds items around a perfect symptom match with a forbidden drug.

checks.q: A 25-year-old with a spinal injury has a BP of 84/50, a heart rate of 52, and warm dry skin below the nipple line. What type of shock is this?
choices: Hypovolemic
Cardiogenic
Neurogenic
Anaphylactic
checks.why: Loss of sympathetic tone from the spinal injury prevents both vasoconstriction and compensatory tachycardia, giving hypotension with a slow rate and warm dry skin. Hypovolemic shock produces cool clammy skin and tachycardia.

checks.q: What is the minimum acceptable systolic blood pressure for a 5-year-old?
choices: 70 mmHg
75 mmHg
80 mmHg
90 mmHg
checks.why: The formula for ages 1 to 10 is 70 plus twice the age in years: 70 plus 10 equals 80 mmHg. Anything lower represents decompensated shock in that child.

checks.q: A patient with classic cardiac chest pain took Cialis last night. Which action is correct?
choices: Assist with nitroglycerin because the indication is clear
Give aspirin and withhold nitroglycerin
Withhold both aspirin and nitroglycerin
Give nitroglycerin at half the usual dose
checks.why: Tadalafil contraindicates nitroglycerin for 48 hours, but nothing about it affects aspirin, which is the intervention with proven mortality benefit. Withholding both would deny a life-saving drug for no reason.

lessons.title: Most-missed topics: trauma, triage and operations
lessons.body:
## Trauma essentials

**Mechanism of injury** drives your index of suspicion. Significant mechanisms include ejection, a death in the same compartment, a fall greater than `20 feet` for adults or `10 feet` or three times the child's height for children, rollover, intrusion over `12 inches`, being struck as a pedestrian, and penetrating trauma to the head, neck, chest or abdomen.

**Bleeding control, in order:** direct pressure, then a **tourniquet** for extremity bleeding that pressure does not stop. Apply it `2 to 3 inches` above the wound, never over a joint, tighten until the bleeding stops, and write the time. Do not loosen it. For junctional wounds at the neck, groin or armpit, pack the wound with a hemostatic dressing and hold pressure.

**Chest injuries:** an open chest wound gets an occlusive dressing; if the patient worsens, burp or remove it because a tension pneumothorax may be developing. Flail chest is two or more ribs broken in two or more places with paradoxical motion — treat with ventilation support, not with weights or straps.

**Head injuries:** a rising blood pressure with a falling heart rate and irregular breathing is **Cushing's triad**, a sign of rising pressure in the skull. Ventilate at a normal rate unless herniation signs are present and your protocol directs otherwise.

**Spinal care:** current practice is selective immobilization. A rigid collar with manual stabilization and a padded stretcher has replaced routine long-board use in most systems. Immobilize when there is midline tenderness, neurological deficit, altered mental status, intoxication, or a distracting injury.

**Burns:** the rule of nines for an adult is `9%` per head, per arm, per half of each leg front and back, `18%` for the front torso and `18%` for the back, and `1%` for the genitals. For a child, the head counts `18%` and each leg `13.5%`. Stop the burning, remove jewelry and non-adherent clothing, cover with a dry sterile dressing, keep the patient warm, and expect fluid loss. Do not apply ice or ointments.

> **Trap:** Burn patients get cold fast, because the skin that keeps heat in is gone. The instinct to cool a large burn causes hypothermia. Cool briefly, then cover and keep them warm.

## START triage

Used when patients outnumber rescuers. Move through fast, do not treat beyond opening an airway and controlling massive bleeding, and tag.

1. **Walking wounded** — direct them to one area. They are **Minor (green)**.
2. **Respirations:** none after opening the airway means **Expectant (black)**. Over `30/min` means **Immediate (red)**.
3. **Perfusion:** absent radial pulse, or capillary refill over `2 seconds`, means **Immediate (red)**.
4. **Mental status:** cannot follow simple commands means **Immediate (red)**.
5. Everyone else is **Delayed (yellow)**.

**JumpSTART** is the pediatric version for children under about `8`: an apneic child with a pulse gets `5` rescue breaths before being tagged expectant, and the respiratory cutoffs are under `15` or over `45` per minute.

## Ambulance operations and the law

**Driving.** Lights and sirens request the right of way, they do not grant it. You must drive with **due regard** for everyone else at all times. Most ambulance collisions happen at intersections, so clear each lane separately and expect that nobody heard you.

**Negligence** requires four elements, all of them: a **duty to act**, a **breach** of the standard of care, **causation** linking the breach to the harm, and actual **damages**. Missing any one means no negligence.

**Abandonment** is terminating care without transferring the patient to someone of equal or higher training. **Consent** is expressed for an alert adult, implied for an unresponsive patient, and given by a parent or guardian for a minor except in an emergency.

**Refusals** require that the patient is an alert, oriented adult with decision-making capacity who has been told the risks in plain words. Document what you told them, that they understood, and who witnessed it.

**Scope of practice** is what the state allows you to do. **Standard of care** is what a reasonable EMT with similar training would do in the same situation. **HIPAA** limits what you share; treatment, payment and operations are permitted uses.

> **On the exam:** Operations items are usually about safety and legality, not medicine. When an item involves a decision that could hurt someone else on the road or violate a patient's rights, the conservative, documented, by-the-book choice is the answer.
keyPoints: Direct pressure first, tourniquet 2 to 3 inches above an extremity wound that will not stop, note the time, do not loosen.
Cushing's triad is rising blood pressure, falling heart rate and irregular breathing — rising intracranial pressure.
Rule of nines: adult head 9%, child head 18%; keep burn patients warm after cooling briefly.
START: walking is green, no breathing after airway opened is black, RR over 30 or no radial pulse or cannot follow commands is red, everyone else yellow.
Negligence needs all four of duty, breach, causation and damages; lights and sirens request right of way, they do not grant it.

checks.q: At a bus crash you reach a patient who is breathing 36 times per minute with a strong radial pulse who follows commands. What START category applies?
choices: Minor (green)
Delayed (yellow)
Immediate (red)
Expectant (black)
checks.why: A respiratory rate over 30 alone makes the patient immediate in START, regardless of how good the pulse and mental status look. The algorithm stops at the first abnormal finding.

checks.q: An EMT stops care and leaves a patient with a bystander before the ambulance arrives. Which concept does this describe?
choices: Abandonment
Implied consent
Breach of confidentiality
Assault
checks.why: Abandonment is terminating care without transferring the patient to a provider of equal or higher training. Consent and confidentiality concern permission and information, not continuity of care.

checks.q: Which set of findings represents Cushing's triad?
choices: Falling blood pressure, rising heart rate, rapid breathing
Rising blood pressure, falling heart rate, irregular breathing
Rising blood pressure, rising heart rate, deep rapid breathing
Falling blood pressure, falling heart rate, warm dry skin
checks.why: As pressure builds inside the skull the body raises blood pressure to keep perfusing the brain, the heart slows reflexively, and the breathing pattern becomes irregular. The last option describes neurogenic shock instead.

lessons.title: The psychomotor exam and the skill stations
lessons.body:
## What is actually happening right now

National Registry certification at the EMT level still takes two things: the cognitive exam, and a **psychomotor (skills) exam**. The skills half is where the confusion lives, because what changed was at the paramedic and AEMT level, not yours.

The National Registry discontinued its own **ALS** psychomotor examination on `July 1, 2024`; paramedic and AEMT skills are now verified through the education program's portfolio. **The BLS psychomotor exam for EMR and EMT did not go away.** It is still required for National Registry certification, and it is established and approved by **each state**, so the format, the site and the scheduling vary: some states run a traditional multi-station exam with outside evaluators, others approve verification inside the accredited course. Your course director tells you which model your state uses.

> **Key:** Whichever model your state uses, the skill sheets and the critical criteria are the same ones below, and the standard is unchanged.

## The stations

**Patient assessment and management, trauma.** A full sequence: scene size-up with standard precautions, mechanism, number of patients, resources, spinal consideration; primary survey with a general impression, level of consciousness, airway, breathing, circulation and a transport decision; then a rapid trauma exam head to toe, baseline vitals, and history.

**Patient assessment and management, medical.** The same shape but driven by history: OPQRST for pain, SAMPLE for history, a focused exam of the relevant system, vitals, and a field impression with a treatment plan.

**Bag-valve-mask ventilation of an apneic adult.** Open the airway, insert an adjunct, ventilate at the correct rate and volume with an adequate seal, connect oxygen at `15 L/min`, and maintain visible chest rise.

**Oxygen administration by nonrebreather.** Assemble the regulator to the tank, crack the cylinder, check the pressure, attach the mask, set `10 to 15 L/min`, pre-fill the reservoir, apply and adjust.

**Cardiac arrest management and AED.** Confirm scene safety, check responsiveness and breathing and pulse together in under `10 seconds`, compressions at `100 to 120/min` at least `2 inches` deep with full recoil, minimal interruptions, attach the AED, clear before analysis and before shock, resume compressions immediately after the shock.

**Bleeding control and shock management.** Direct pressure, then more dressings, then a tourniquet when bleeding continues, then treat for shock with oxygen, position, warmth and transport.

**Long bone immobilization.** Assess distal pulse, motor and sensation before and after; manual stabilization the whole time; splint immobilizing the joint above and below; secure; reassess distal function.

**Joint immobilization.** Same principle, but immobilize the bone above and below the joint, and do not attempt to straighten an injured joint with a pulse present.

**Spinal immobilization, seated and supine.** Manual in-line stabilization from the start and held until the patient is fully secured, correctly sized collar, torso secured before the head, pad voids, reassess distal function before and after.

## The critical criteria that fail you instantly

These are the actions that end a station no matter how well everything else went.

- Failing to take or verbalize **standard precautions**.
- Failing to determine **scene safety**.
- Failing to assess or manage an immediate threat to the airway, breathing or circulation.
- Failing to provide **high-concentration oxygen** when indicated, or interrupting ventilation for more than `30 seconds`.
- Failing to **manually stabilize** the spine and maintain it until the patient is fully secured.
- Securing the **head before the torso** in spinal immobilization.
- Failing to check **distal pulse, motor and sensation** before and after splinting.
- Any action that causes or worsens **patient injury**.
- Exceeding the scope of practice.
- Failing to manage the patient as a competent EMT, or performing a dangerous or unnecessary intervention.

> **Trap:** The two most common instant failures are silence and order. Say 'BSI, scene is safe' out loud at the start of every station, and secure the torso before the head every single time.

## How to practice

Work from the actual skill sheets, out loud, with a timer, and with a partner reading the sheet. Narrate everything you do — an evaluator can only score what they hear or see. Practice the first `30 seconds` of each station until it is automatic, because that is where the critical criteria live.
keyPoints: An EMT still needs a state-approved BLS psychomotor exam plus the cognitive exam; only the ALS (AEMT and paramedic) psychomotor exam was discontinued, on July 1, 2024.
The skill sheets and critical criteria are unchanged regardless of which model your state uses.
Instant failures include missing BSI or scene safety, unmanaged ABC threats, interrupting ventilation over 30 seconds, and securing the head before the torso.
Always check distal pulse, motor and sensation before and after any splinting.
Narrate every action out loud — evaluators score what they hear and see, not what you intended.

checks.q: During the spinal immobilization station you secure the head to the board before strapping the torso. What happens?
choices: Nothing, as long as everything is secure at the end
You lose a point but may continue
It is a critical criterion failure for that station
It is preferred because it protects the cervical spine sooner
checks.why: Securing the head first lets the torso shift underneath it, which moves the neck. Torso before head is a listed critical criterion, and violating it fails the station outright.

checks.q: What must you assess before and after applying any splint?
choices: Blood pressure in the affected limb
Distal pulse, motor function and sensation
Capillary refill only
Skin temperature of the opposite limb
checks.why: Splinting can compress vessels and nerves, so distal pulse, motor and sensory function are documented before and after to detect a change. Omitting either check is a critical failure.

checks.q: Which statement about the EMT psychomotor exam is accurate as of 2026?
choices: It has been eliminated, and EMT skills are no longer verified at all
A state-approved BLS psychomotor exam is still required for EMT certification, and each state sets how it is administered
It is now taken online
It is now required twice per recertification cycle
checks.why: The National Registry discontinued the ALS psychomotor exam for AEMT and paramedic candidates on July 1, 2024, but the BLS psychomotor requirement for EMR and EMT remains and is established and approved by each state. Skills are still verified; only the level above yours changed.

lessons.title: New Jersey certification and staying certified
lessons.body:
Passing the National Registry exam earns you a national certification. Working in New Jersey requires a **state certification**, which is a separate document with its own process. Both matter, and they renew on different clocks.

## Getting certified in New Jersey

1. **Complete an approved EMT course.** New Jersey EMT courses are approved by the **New Jersey Office of Emergency Medical Services (NJ OEMS)** within the Department of Health, and run roughly `190` hours or more of classroom, lab and clinical time depending on the program.
2. **Hold a current CPR card.** A healthcare-provider level BLS card, typically American Heart Association BLS for Healthcare Providers or an equivalent, is required to enter and to finish the course.
3. **Pass the National Registry cognitive exam** at a Pearson VUE center after your course director verifies your completion.
4. **Complete skills verification** through the model your state and program use.
5. **Apply to NJ OEMS for state EMT certification**, including the application, the fee, and a **criminal history background check** with fingerprinting.
6. **Wait.** Processing takes weeks, not days. Apply the moment you are eligible, especially if a job offer depends on the card.

> **On shift:** Hospitals in New Jersey routinely hire emergency department technicians with an EMT certification plus a BLS card, and many will accept a National Registry certification while the state card is pending. Ask; do not assume you have to wait.

## Staying certified

**National Registry recertification** runs on a `2-year` cycle, ending March 31 of even or odd years depending on your initial date. The model is the **National Continued Competency Program (NCCP)**, which for EMT requires `40 hours` of continuing education split three ways:

| Component | Hours | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| National | `20` | Topics the National Registry specifies for the cycle |
| Local or state | `10` | Topics your state or agency requires |
| Individual | `10` | Whatever you choose — your weak areas, or a specialty |

You also maintain a current CPR credential and provide verification from your agency or medical director.

**New Jersey EMT certification** renews on its own schedule with its own continuing-education requirement, currently a three-year cycle. The specific hour requirements have changed in recent years, so confirm the current rule directly with NJ OEMS rather than trusting a study guide, including this one.

> **Key:** Keep a running CEU log from day one: date, topic, hours, provider, and the certificate. Reconstructing two years of education the month before a deadline is a well-known form of misery, and a lost certificate is hours you cannot count.

## Practical habits

- Set a calendar reminder `6 months` before each expiration, not one month.
- Save every certificate as a PDF in one folder, named by date and topic.
- Do the `20` national hours early; they are the most specific and the hardest to find late.
- Count the education your employer already gives you. Hospital and agency in-services usually qualify.
- If you let a certification lapse, the path back is longer and more expensive than renewing on time — in some cases it means retesting.

## Two cards, two clocks

The common mistake is assuming that renewing one renews the other. National Registry certification proves competence nationally. New Jersey certification is what allows you to work in New Jersey. Track both, and remember that your employer's credential file wants copies of both plus your CPR card.
keyPoints: New Jersey certification requires an NJ OEMS-approved course of roughly 190 hours, a healthcare-provider CPR card, the NREMT cognitive exam, skills verification, an application with a fee, and a background check.
National Registry recertification is a 2-year cycle using the NCCP 40-hour model: 20 national, 10 local, 10 individual.
New Jersey certification renews on its own cycle, currently three years — confirm current hour requirements with NJ OEMS.
Keep a CEU log with date, topic, hours, provider and certificate from day one.
National and state certifications are two separate cards on two separate clocks; renewing one does not renew the other.

checks.q: How many continuing education hours does the NCCP model require for EMT recertification, and how are they divided?
choices: 24 hours, all individual choice
40 hours: 20 national, 10 local or state, 10 individual
72 hours: 36 national and 36 local
40 hours, all national component
checks.why: The National Continued Competency Program splits 40 hours into a 20-hour national component, a 10-hour local or state component, and 10 individual hours you choose. It is not a single pool.

checks.q: You renewed your National Registry certification. What is true about your New Jersey certification?
choices: It renews automatically with the National Registry
It is no longer required once you are nationally registered
It is a separate certification on its own cycle that must be renewed separately
It only needs renewal if you change employers
checks.why: National and state certifications are independent documents with independent renewal cycles. National Registry proves competence; the state card is what authorizes you to work in New Jersey.

lessons.title: The four-week plan, exam day, and the job after
lessons.body:
## Why rereading fails

Rereading a chapter feels productive because the material becomes familiar, and familiarity feels like knowledge. It is not. The only thing that builds durable recall is **retrieving** information from your own memory, repeatedly, with gaps in between. That means practice questions and flashcards, not highlighting.

Two rules carry the whole plan. **Spaced retrieval:** review material at expanding intervals rather than in one block. **Question-first study:** attempt a question before you review the topic, even if you get it wrong — the failed attempt is what makes the correction stick.

## Four weeks

**Week 1 — map and baseline.** Take a `50`-question mixed practice set cold, before studying. Score it by domain. That profile is your syllabus. Then work the two biggest domains: Medical and OB-GYN, and Cardiology and Resuscitation. Every study session ends with `25` questions.

**Week 2 — airway and trauma.** Airway is the densest pile of memorizable numbers in the course, and airway items sit inside Primary Assessment, the biggest domain on the test. Trauma is thinner but the sequence questions come from it. Build flashcards for every number you miss, and review yesterday's cards before starting new material. End each session with `25` questions.

**Week 3 — operations and weak spots.** Operations is small but high-yield because it is pure recall: driving, legal, triage, hazardous materials, incident command, lifting and moving. Then go back to whatever your week-one profile said was weakest. Start doing `50`-question sets in one sitting.

**Week 4 — simulate and taper.** Two or three full-length `120`-question sessions under real conditions: timed, no phone, no notes, no pausing. Review every question you missed **and** every one you guessed right. In the last two days, review only your own flashcards and error log. Do not learn new material the day before.

**The error log** is the whole trick. For every question you miss, write one line: the topic, why you missed it, and the correct rule. Review that list weekly. Most people miss the same twelve things over and over.

> **Key:** If you can do `50` mixed questions and explain out loud why each wrong answer is wrong, you are ready. Reading the book again will not move that number.

## Exam day

- Bring two forms of identification, one of them a **government-issued photo ID with your signature**, with names matching your National Registry account exactly.
- Arrive `30 minutes` early. Late arrival usually means forfeiting the fee.
- Everything goes in a locker: phone, watch, food, notes, hat. Expect a check before you enter.
- **Pacing:** you have `2 hours` for `70 to 120` questions, so about `1 minute` each. Most people finish with time left. If you are consistently over `90 seconds`, you are overthinking.
- **Breaks** come out of your exam time on this test. Plan around that.
- **You cannot go back.** The adaptive format locks each answer, so there is no flagging and no review. Commit and move.
- **Do not change an answer without a reason.** Changing based on a rule you can name is fine. Changing because a choice 'feels' better usually turns a right answer into a wrong one — and you cannot do it here anyway, so trust your first read.
- If you blank, reread the last line of the stem and ask which choice comes first in the priority order.

## After you pass: the ED technician job

Emergency department technician, ER tech and patient care technician are largely the same role with different titles. The job is vital signs, EKGs, phlebotomy and specimen handling, splinting, wound care setup, Foley catheters in some departments, point-of-care testing, transporting patients, stocking, turning and cleaning patients, and being the extra pair of hands in a code.

**What postings ask for:** an EMT-B certification and a current BLS card, almost always. Listed as a plus: phlebotomy certification, EKG technician certification, prior patient-care experience, and a CNA background. Many New Jersey hospitals will hire on the National Registry card while the state certification processes.

**What to say in the interview.** They are screening for three things: will you show up, can you take direction in a chaotic room, and will you tell someone when a patient looks worse. Give concrete examples. Say that you escalate early. Ask what their orientation and competency checklist covers.

**Orientation** typically runs one to three weeks: hospital onboarding, electronic charting, the department's own competencies such as EKG placement and blood draws, and a preceptorship on the floor before you take your own assignments.

> **On shift:** The technician who gets kept is the one who says 'bed 12 looks worse than ten minutes ago' out loud. Nobody expects you to diagnose. They expect you to notice and to speak.
keyPoints: Retrieval practice beats rereading: do questions first, then study what you missed.
Four weeks: baseline and biggest domains, then airway and trauma, then operations and weak spots, then full-length timed simulations.
Keep an error log of topic, reason missed and the correct rule — most people miss the same dozen things repeatedly.
Exam day: two IDs, arrive 30 minutes early, about 1 minute per question, breaks come out of your time, and answers cannot be changed.
ED tech postings want EMT plus BLS, with phlebotomy or EKG certification as a plus; many NJ hospitals hire on the NREMT card while the state card processes.

checks.q: Which study method builds the most durable recall for this exam?
choices: Rereading the chapter until it feels familiar
Highlighting key terms in a study guide
Attempting practice questions, then reviewing what you missed, spaced over days
Watching lecture videos at double speed
checks.why: Retrieving information from memory and spacing that retrieval over time is what builds durable recall. Rereading and highlighting produce familiarity, which feels like knowledge but does not survive an exam.

checks.q: You are 40 questions into the exam and feel like you are failing. What should you do?
choices: Continue answering normally, because feeling that way is the expected experience on an adaptive exam
Start guessing quickly to finish before the clock runs out
Take a long break to reset
Deliberately answer a few wrong so the questions get easier
checks.why: The adaptive algorithm targets the edge of your ability, so passing candidates feel uncertain most of the way through. Breaks come out of your time, and deliberately answering wrong lowers your ability estimate toward failing.

checks.q: Which combination is most commonly required in an emergency department technician job posting?
choices: Paramedic certification and an associate degree
EMT certification and a current BLS card
Nursing license and ACLS
Phlebotomy certification only
checks.why: EMT plus a current healthcare-provider BLS card is the standard baseline, with phlebotomy or EKG certification listed as preferred extras rather than requirements.

cards.front: How many questions and how much time does the EMT cognitive exam allow?
cards.back: A minimum of 70 and a maximum of 120 questions in 2 hours total, including any break you take. Some items are unscored pilot questions.

cards.front: How does a computer-adaptive test decide when to stop?
cards.back: When it is 95 percent confident your ability is above or below the passing standard, or when you reach the question limit or the time limit. Early shutoff means confidence, not necessarily success.

cards.front: What are the five NREMT content domains and their weights?
cards.back: Under the test plan effective April 7, 2025: Scene Size-Up and Safety 15-19 percent; Primary Assessment 39-43; Secondary Assessment 5-9; Patient Treatment and Transport 20-24; Operations 10-14.

cards.front: How is pediatric content distributed on the exam?
cards.back: Pediatric items are integrated throughout the examination content rather than assigned a fixed percentage, so a child can appear in any domain.

cards.front: How long must you wait to retest after a failed attempt, and how many attempts do you get?
cards.back: Fifteen days between attempts. Three attempts, then documented remedial training, then three more, for a maximum of six before the course must be repeated.

cards.front: What do the cue words 'first' and 'next' mean in a question stem?
cards.back: 'First' asks what comes earliest in the sequence right now. 'Next' assumes everything before it is already done and asks what follows.

cards.front: When does 'assess' beat 'treat' as the correct answer?
cards.back: When the stem has not told you the airway, breathing and circulation status. Treatment answers become correct only once assessment findings are already given to you.

cards.front: When is 'transport immediately' the right answer?
cards.back: When the problem cannot be fixed by any EMT skill: internal bleeding, prolapsed cord, limb presentation, ectopic pregnancy, an intracranial bleed, anything needing surgery.

cards.front: When is 'call for ALS' the right answer, and when is it not?
cards.back: Right when the patient needs a drug or skill above EMT level. Wrong as the first action when an immediate life threat is untreated — ventilate or control bleeding first, then call.

cards.front: What four assumptions does the NREMT expect you to make?
cards.back: You have a partner, a fully equipped BLS ambulance, standing orders for the EMT scope, and you answer from the national standard of care rather than local protocol.

cards.front: State the priority order for any 'what do you do first' question.
cards.back: Scene safety, standard precautions, general impression and level of consciousness, airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure, then history, vitals and everything else.

cards.front: What are the two exceptions to airway-before-everything?
cards.back: Massive external hemorrhage is controlled first (the X in XABC), and adult cardiac arrest starts with compressions (CAB). Newborn arrest is the reverse — ventilation leads.

cards.front: How do you tell adequate from inadequate breathing, and what does each require?
cards.back: Judge rate and depth together. Adequate breathing with low saturation gets titrated oxygen; inadequate breathing — slow, shallow or agonal — gets assisted ventilation with a BVM.

cards.front: What are the five components of scene size-up?
cards.back: Scene safety, standard precautions, mechanism of injury or nature of illness, number of patients, and the need for additional resources.

cards.front: What is the rescue-breathing rate for an adult with a pulse but no breathing?
cards.back: One breath every 6 seconds, about 10 per minute. For infants and children with a pulse it is one breath every 2 to 3 seconds, about 20 to 30 per minute.

cards.front: When do you use an OPA versus an NPA?
cards.back: An OPA requires no gag reflex; an NPA is tolerated with one. Avoid an NPA with suspected skull fracture or significant facial trauma.

cards.front: How do you size an OPA and an NPA?
cards.back: OPA: corner of the mouth to the earlobe or angle of the jaw. NPA: nostril to the earlobe, lubricated, bevel toward the septum, inserted straight back along the floor of the nose.

cards.front: What are the maximum suction times by age?
cards.back: 10 to 15 seconds for an adult, 10 seconds for a child, 5 seconds for an infant. Suction on the way out and reoxygenate between attempts.

cards.front: State the compression rate and depth for adults, children and infants.
cards.back: Rate 100 to 120 per minute for all. Depth at least 2 inches and not over 2.4 in adults, about 2 inches or one third of the chest in children, about 1.5 inches in infants.

cards.front: What are the CPR ratios for one and two rescuers by age?
cards.back: Adults are 30:2 with one or two rescuers. Children and infants are 30:2 with one rescuer and 15:2 with two rescuers. Newborn resuscitation is 3:1.

cards.front: What do you do immediately after an AED delivers a shock?
cards.back: Resume chest compressions immediately without checking a pulse, continue for 2 minutes, then allow the AED to reanalyze. Switch compressors every 2 minutes.

cards.front: Name four AED pad placement cautions.
cards.back: Dry a wet chest, move the patient off standing water and metal, avoid placing pads over a pacemaker bulge, and remove medication patches before applying pads.

cards.front: How does left-sided heart failure differ from right-sided on exam?
cards.back: Left-sided backs fluid into the lungs: crackles, pink frothy sputum, orthopnea. Right-sided backs fluid into the body: ankle edema, distended neck veins, enlarged liver.

cards.front: What three things does a stroke question always want?
cards.back: Use a stroke scale to identify the deficit, establish the last known well time, and transport to a stroke center with early notification. Aspirin is not given for stroke.

cards.front: What is the minimum systolic blood pressure formula for children 1 to 10 years?
cards.back: 70 plus twice the age in years. A 5-year-old needs at least 80 mmHg; below that is decompensated shock.

cards.front: What does bradycardia in a child mean, and what is the treatment?
cards.back: Hypoxia until proven otherwise, and a pre-arrest sign. Treat with oxygenation and assisted ventilation, not observation.

cards.front: What three findings mean delivery is imminent?
cards.back: Crowning, an overwhelming urge to push, and contractions 2 to 3 minutes apart lasting 60 to 90 seconds. Crowning alone means deliver on scene.

cards.front: Distinguish placenta previa from abruptio placentae in one line each.
cards.back: Previa is painless bright red bleeding with a soft uterus. Abruption is painful dark bleeding with a rigid tender uterus, often after trauma, and may be concealed.

cards.front: What are the newborn resuscitation thresholds?
cards.back: Apnea or heart rate under 100 means ventilate at 40 to 60 per minute. Heart rate under 60 after 30 seconds of effective ventilation means compressions at 3:1, 120 events per minute.

cards.front: Why does blood pressure fall last in shock?
cards.back: The body compensates by constricting vessels and raising heart rate, holding pressure until volume loss is severe. Judge by heart rate, skin, capillary refill and mental status instead.

cards.front: What makes neurogenic shock look different from every other kind?
cards.back: Hypotension with bradycardia and warm, dry, flushed skin, because the injured cord cannot signal vessels to constrict or the heart to speed up. Every other shock gives tachycardia and cool skin.

cards.front: List the contraindications to nitroglycerin.
cards.back: Systolic under 100 per protocol, a PDE-5 inhibitor within 24 hours (sildenafil, vardenafil) or 48 hours (tadalafil), head injury or raised intracranial pressure, three doses already given, and allergy.

cards.front: List the contraindications to aspirin in the field.
cards.back: Known allergy, active GI bleeding or ulcer, recent hemorrhagic stroke, known bleeding disorder, and children or teens with fever or viral illness because of Reye syndrome.

cards.front: Which mechanisms of injury count as significant?
cards.back: Ejection, a death in the same compartment, falls over 20 feet for adults or 10 feet or three times height for children, rollover, intrusion over 12 inches, pedestrian struck, and penetrating trauma to head, neck, chest or abdomen.

cards.front: How do you apply a tourniquet correctly?
cards.back: After direct pressure fails, place it 2 to 3 inches above the wound, never over a joint, tighten until bleeding stops, note the time, and do not loosen it.

cards.front: What do you do if a patient with an occlusive dressing on a chest wound gets worse?
cards.back: Burp or remove the dressing. A tension pneumothorax may be building, and releasing the seal lets trapped air escape.

cards.front: What is Cushing's triad and what does it indicate?
cards.back: Rising blood pressure, falling heart rate and irregular breathing — a late sign of rising pressure inside the skull. It is a load-and-go finding.

cards.front: State the rule of nines for an adult and how a child differs.
cards.back: Adult: 9 percent each for head, each arm, and each half-leg front and back; 18 percent front torso, 18 percent back, 1 percent genitals. A child's head is 18 percent and each leg is 13.5.

cards.front: Why do burn patients become hypothermic, and what does that change?
cards.back: The damaged skin can no longer hold heat in. Cool the burn only briefly, then cover with dry sterile dressings and actively keep the patient warm.

cards.front: Walk through the START triage algorithm.
cards.back: Walking wounded are green. No breathing after opening the airway is black. Respirations over 30, no radial pulse or capillary refill over 2 seconds, or inability to follow commands is red. Everyone else is yellow.

cards.front: What are the four elements of negligence?
cards.back: Duty to act, breach of the standard of care, causation linking the breach to the harm, and actual damages. All four must be present.

cards.front: What is abandonment?
cards.back: Terminating patient care without transferring the patient to a provider of equal or higher training. Leaving a patient with a bystander or a lower-level provider qualifies.

cards.front: What is the difference between scope of practice and standard of care?
cards.back: Scope of practice is what the state legally allows you to do. Standard of care is what a reasonable EMT with similar training would do in the same situation.

cards.front: What do lights and sirens actually grant you?
cards.back: Nothing legally except a request for the right of way. You must always drive with due regard, and most ambulance collisions happen at intersections where other drivers did not yield.

cards.front: What must be true for a patient refusal to be valid?
cards.back: The patient is an alert, oriented adult with decision-making capacity who has been informed of the risks in plain language. Document what you said, that they understood, and a witness.

cards.front: What changed about the psychomotor exam in 2024, and what did not?
cards.back: The National Registry discontinued the ALS (AEMT and paramedic) psychomotor exam on July 1, 2024. The BLS psychomotor exam for EMR and EMT is still required and is approved by each state.

cards.front: Name five critical criteria that instantly fail a skill station.
cards.back: Failing to take standard precautions or determine scene safety, failing to manage an ABC threat, interrupting ventilation over 30 seconds, securing the head before the torso, and omitting distal pulse, motor and sensory checks.

cards.front: What order do you secure a patient during spinal immobilization?
cards.back: Manual in-line stabilization first and held throughout, correctly sized collar, torso secured before the head, voids padded, then distal function reassessed. Head before torso is an instant failure.

cards.front: What does the long bone immobilization station require before and after splinting?
cards.back: Assess distal pulse, motor function and sensation before and after. Maintain manual stabilization throughout and immobilize the joint above and below the fracture.

cards.front: Why must you narrate everything during a skill station?
cards.back: Evaluators score what they see and hear. Actions you perform silently, including BSI and scene safety, may not be credited and can trigger a critical criteria failure.

cards.front: What are the steps to New Jersey EMT certification?
cards.back: Complete an NJ OEMS-approved course of roughly 190 hours, hold a healthcare-provider CPR card, pass the NREMT cognitive exam, complete skills verification, then apply to NJ OEMS with a fee and background check.

cards.front: What is the NCCP 40-hour model?
cards.back: The National Continued Competency Program for EMT recertification: 20 hours of the national component, 10 hours local or state, and 10 individual hours, every 2 years.

cards.front: Do National Registry and New Jersey certifications renew together?
cards.back: No. They are separate documents on separate cycles — National Registry every 2 years, New Jersey on its own multi-year cycle. Renewing one does not renew the other.

cards.front: Why does retrieval practice beat rereading?
cards.back: Rereading builds familiarity, which feels like knowledge but fades. Pulling information out of memory, repeatedly and with gaps between attempts, is what creates durable recall.

cards.front: What is an error log and how do you use it?
cards.back: One line per missed question: the topic, why you missed it, and the correct rule. Reviewed weekly, it reveals that most candidates miss the same dozen things repeatedly.

cards.front: What is the right pacing target on exam day?
cards.back: About 1 minute per question, since you have 2 hours for 70 to 120 items. Consistently spending over 90 seconds means you are overthinking.

cards.front: Can you flag a question or change an answer on the NREMT exam?
cards.back: No. The adaptive format locks each answer as you submit it, so there is no flagging and no going back. Commit to your first reasoned read and move on.

cards.front: What identification do you need at the Pearson VUE center?
cards.back: Two forms of identification, one a government-issued photo ID with your signature, with the name matching your National Registry account exactly. Arrive 30 minutes early.

cards.front: What do emergency department technician job postings typically require?
cards.back: EMT certification plus a current BLS card. Listed as preferred: phlebotomy certification, EKG technician certification, and prior patient-care experience such as CNA work.

cards.front: What are ED technicians actually doing on a shift?
cards.back: Vital signs, EKGs, phlebotomy and specimens, splinting, wound care setup, point-of-care testing, transporting patients, turning and cleaning, stocking, and extra hands during a code.

quiz.q: A 58-year-old is found unresponsive, snoring loudly, with a strong radial pulse. What should you do first?
choices: Open the airway with a head-tilt chin-lift
Apply a nonrebreather at 15 L/min
Obtain a blood pressure
Insert an oropharyngeal airway
quiz.why: Snoring is the tongue obstructing the airway, and positioning fixes it in a second with no equipment. Oxygen cannot flow through an obstructed airway, an adjunct comes after positioning, and vitals wait for the primary survey to finish.

quiz.q: An unresponsive patient with a suspected basilar skull fracture and clear fluid draining from the nose needs an airway adjunct. Which is appropriate?
choices: Nasopharyngeal airway
Oropharyngeal airway
Either one is acceptable
No adjunct should be used
quiz.why: An NPA is contraindicated with a suspected skull fracture because it could pass through the fracture. An unresponsive patient without a gag reflex tolerates an OPA, and leaving an unresponsive patient with no adjunct abandons the airway.

quiz.q: A 24-year-old asthmatic is breathing 32 times per minute with shallow chest movement, one-word speech, and a saturation of 88% on a nonrebreather. What is the appropriate action?
choices: Increase the nonrebreather flow to 25 L/min
Coach her to slow her breathing
Begin assisted ventilations with a bag-valve mask
Place a nasal cannula under the mask
quiz.why: Fast and shallow with one-word speech is inadequate ventilation, and a mask only helps someone moving air. Assisted ventilation is the treatment; raising the flow above 15 L/min adds nothing.

quiz.q: How long may you suction an adult patient's airway at one time?
choices: 5 seconds
30 seconds
60 seconds
10 to 15 seconds
quiz.why: Suctioning removes oxygen along with secretions, so adult attempts are limited to 10 to 15 seconds, with 10 for a child and 5 for an infant, reoxygenating between attempts.

quiz.q: A COPD patient in moderate distress has a room-air saturation of 85%. What is the most appropriate oxygen therapy?
choices: Withhold oxygen because of the hypoxic drive
Titrate oxygen to a saturation of 88 to 92%
Nonrebreather at 15 L/min until the saturation reaches 100%
Nasal cannula at 0.5 L/min regardless of the saturation
quiz.why: COPD patients are treated to a target of 88 to 92%, which means giving oxygen at 85% but not driving it to 100%. Withholding oxygen from a hypoxic patient is never correct.

quiz.q: An adult is in cardiac arrest. Your AED delivers a shock. What is the next step?
choices: Check for a carotid pulse for 10 seconds
Give two ventilations
Resume chest compressions immediately
Allow the AED to reanalyze
quiz.why: Compressions resume immediately after a shock because a recently converted heart still needs perfusion and every pause lowers survival. The AED reanalyzes after 2 minutes of CPR.

quiz.q: Two EMTs are performing CPR on a 4-year-old. What compression-to-ventilation ratio applies?
quiz.why: Two-rescuer child CPR uses 15:2 because children arrest from respiratory causes and need more ventilation. Single-rescuer child CPR remains 30:2, and 3:1 applies to newborn resuscitation.

quiz.q: A 62-year-old has crushing substernal chest pain, a BP of 148/88, and takes no erectile dysfunction medication. He has no aspirin allergy and no bleeding history. What is the priority medication?
choices: Oral glucose
Albuterol
Activated charcoal
Aspirin 324 mg chewed
quiz.why: Chewed aspirin is the prehospital intervention with proven mortality benefit in acute coronary syndrome, and no contraindication is present. The other three treat entirely different conditions.

quiz.q: A 70-year-old with a cardiac history has crackles in both lung bases, pink frothy sputum, and severe dyspnea when lying flat. What is happening?
choices: Left-sided heart failure with pulmonary edema
Right-sided heart failure
Pneumothorax
Hyperventilation syndrome
quiz.why: Left ventricular failure backs fluid into the lungs, producing crackles, frothy sputum and orthopnea. Right-sided failure backs fluid into the body instead, giving ankle edema and distended neck veins.

quiz.q: A 66-year-old has sudden right-sided weakness and slurred speech that began at an unknown time. His wife last saw him normal at 8 p.m. What is the most important information to obtain and report?
choices: His full medication list before departing
His pain score
The last known well time of 8 p.m.
Whether he has eaten today
quiz.why: Time-sensitive stroke treatment is based on the last known well time, which determines eligibility for clot-dissolving therapy. Everything else can be gathered en route or at the hospital.

quiz.q: A patient in cardiac arrest has a nitroglycerin patch on the left upper chest where you want to place an AED pad. What should you do?
choices: Place the pad directly over the patch
Remove the patch with a gloved hand, wipe the area, and place the pad
Place both pads on the back instead
Do not use the AED
quiz.why: A medication patch can block energy delivery and cause skin burns, so it is removed with a glove to avoid dosing yourself. Withholding defibrillation or improvising pad placement both reduce the chance of survival.

quiz.q: A 2-year-old has a heart rate of 54 and slow shallow respirations after a near-drowning. What does the heart rate indicate?
choices: A vagal response to cold water
Normal for a sleeping toddler
Severe hypoxia requiring immediate ventilation
An expected finding after a scare
quiz.why: Children become bradycardic from hypoxia, and it is a pre-arrest sign. The treatment is ventilation and oxygenation, not observation, and a normal toddler rate is 90 to 150.

quiz.q: What is the minimum acceptable systolic blood pressure for a 7-year-old?
choices: 70 mmHg
77 mmHg
84 mmHg
90 mmHg
quiz.why: Use 70 plus twice the age in years for ages 1 to 10: 70 plus 14 equals 84 mmHg. A pressure below that in a child represents decompensated shock and imminent arrest.

quiz.q: A 25-year-old on her third pregnancy is crowning with contractions 2 minutes apart. The hospital is 12 minutes away. What should you do?
choices: Transport emergently and deliver at the hospital
Prepare to deliver on scene
Have her hold her legs together during transport
Place her in knee-chest position and transport
quiz.why: Crowning means the head is at the outlet, and a third delivery progresses rapidly. Delaying or physically restraining a delivery risks fetal hypoxia and maternal injury; knee-chest is for a prolapsed cord.

quiz.q: A 34-week pregnant patient has painful dark vaginal bleeding with a rigid, tender uterus after a car crash. What do you suspect?
choices: Placenta previa
Normal labor
Abruptio placentae
Ruptured ectopic pregnancy
quiz.why: Pain with a rigid uterus after trauma is abruption, where the placenta shears off the wall and much of the bleeding may be concealed. Previa is painless with a soft uterus, and labor pain comes in waves.

quiz.q: A newborn remains apneic with a heart rate of 80 after drying, warming, positioning and stimulation. What is the next step?
choices: Chest compressions at 3:1
Blow-by oxygen and reassess in one minute
Deep tracheal suctioning
Positive-pressure ventilation at 40 to 60 breaths per minute
quiz.why: Apnea or a heart rate under 100 after the initial steps means ventilate, which is the highest-yield newborn intervention. Compressions wait until the rate stays under 60 after 30 seconds of effective ventilation.

quiz.q: A 21-year-old with a cervical spine injury has a BP of 80/48, a heart rate of 50, and warm dry skin. What kind of shock is this?
choices: Neurogenic
Hypovolemic
Cardiogenic
Septic
quiz.why: Loss of sympathetic tone prevents both vasoconstriction and compensatory tachycardia, giving hypotension with bradycardia and warm dry skin. Every other shock type produces tachycardia with cool clammy skin.

quiz.q: A patient with chest pain took sildenafil 10 hours ago and has a BP of 152/90. Which statement is correct?
choices: Nitroglycerin is safe because the pressure is high
Nitroglycerin is contraindicated for 24 hours after sildenafil
Aspirin is contraindicated because of the sildenafil
Both aspirin and nitroglycerin are contraindicated
quiz.why: Sildenafil and vardenafil block nitroglycerin for 24 hours and tadalafil for 48, and a high starting pressure does not prevent the resulting collapse. Sildenafil has no interaction with aspirin, which should still be given.

quiz.q: An unresponsive diabetic patient has a glucose of 34 mg/dL and no gag reflex. What is the appropriate EMT action?
choices: Place oral glucose gel between the cheek and gum
Place a sugar packet under the tongue
Manage the airway and request ALS for IV dextrose
Pour juice slowly into the mouth
quiz.why: Anything placed in the mouth of a patient without a gag reflex will be aspirated, which is an absolute contraindication to oral glucose in any form. Airway management plus ALS is the correct path.

quiz.q: A 40-year-old has hives, wheezing, swollen lips and a BP of 78/44 after a wasp sting. What is the priority intervention?
choices: Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM in the anterolateral thigh
Albuterol by nebulizer
Oral diphenhydramine
A cold pack to the sting site
quiz.why: This is anaphylaxis with both airway and circulatory involvement, and epinephrine is the only drug that reverses vasodilation, bronchospasm and swelling at once. Albuterol and antihistamines are adjuncts and too slow to be the priority.

quiz.q: A patient found in a garage with a running car is confused, with a pulse oximetry reading of 98% on room air. What is the correct action?
choices: Withhold oxygen because the saturation is normal
Apply a nasal cannula at 2 L/min
Apply a nonrebreather at 15 L/min regardless of the reading
Check a blood glucose and reassess in 10 minutes
quiz.why: A standard pulse oximeter cannot distinguish carbon monoxide from oxygen on hemoglobin, so it reads falsely high. High-flow oxygen speeds carbon monoxide elimination, and the reading is ignored entirely.

quiz.q: A 30-year-old has arterial bleeding from a mid-thigh laceration that does not stop with direct pressure. What is the next step?
choices: Apply a pressure dressing and elevate the leg
Apply a tourniquet 2 to 3 inches above the wound and note the time
Apply pressure to the femoral artery for 10 minutes
Pack the wound and apply ice
quiz.why: When direct pressure fails on an extremity, a tourniquet goes on proximal to the wound, tightened until the bleeding stops, with the time documented. Elevation and pressure points are no longer taught as effective steps.

quiz.q: A head-injured patient's vitals trend from BP 132/78, HR 88 to BP 186/70, HR 48 with irregular breathing. What does this indicate?
choices: Improving perfusion
Hypovolemic shock
Rising intracranial pressure (Cushing's triad)
A vasovagal episode
quiz.why: The body raises blood pressure to keep perfusing a compressed brain, the heart slows reflexively, and breathing becomes irregular. This is a late and ominous sign that demands rapid transport to a trauma center.

quiz.q: At a multi-casualty scene you find a patient breathing 12 times per minute with a radial pulse who cannot follow simple commands. What START category applies?
choices: Minor (green)
Delayed (yellow)
