Expectant (black)
Immediate (red)
quiz.why: Inability to follow commands is the mental status criterion that makes a patient immediate, even with a normal rate and a present radial pulse. START tags on the first abnormal finding and moves on.

quiz.q: An adult has partial-thickness burns to the entire front of the torso and the entire right arm. What percentage of body surface area is burned using the rule of nines?
quiz.why: The front of the torso is 18% and an entire arm is 9%, totaling 27%. The 36% figure would require adding the back as well, and 18% alone omits the arm.

quiz.q: An EMT transfers a patient to a first-aid volunteer with less training and leaves the scene. Which legal concept applies?
choices: Abandonment
Negligence per se
Breach of confidentiality
Implied consent
quiz.why: Abandonment is ending care without handing the patient to someone of equal or higher training. Negligence would require proving duty, breach, causation and damages, and confidentiality concerns information rather than continuity.

quiz.q: You are responding with lights and sirens and approach a red light at a busy intersection. What is required?
choices: Proceed because emergency vehicles have the right of way
Increase the siren volume and continue at speed
Come to a controlled stop or slow enough to clear each lane individually before proceeding
Turn off the lights and proceed normally
quiz.why: Lights and sirens request the right of way; they do not grant it, and due regard is required at all times. Intersections are where most ambulance collisions happen because drivers do not hear or yield.

quiz.q: An alert, oriented 45-year-old with chest pain refuses transport. What must you do for the refusal to be valid?
choices: Have a family member sign for him
Transport him anyway under implied consent
Simply note 'patient refused' in the chart
Explain the specific risks in plain language, confirm he understands, document it, and obtain a witness
quiz.why: A valid refusal requires an adult with capacity who has been informed of the specific risks and understands them, documented with a witness. Implied consent applies only to patients who cannot consent for themselves.

quiz.q: You arrive at a domestic violence call. The patient is on the porch and a man is yelling from inside the house. Police are en route. What do you do?
choices: Stage at a safe distance until law enforcement secures the scene
Move the patient into the ambulance quickly
Enter and begin assessment while your partner watches the door
Ask the man to come outside and calm down
quiz.why: Scene safety precedes all patient care, and an active, unsecured violent scene is not entered or approached. An injured crew multiplies the problem and delays care for everyone.

quiz.q: A trauma patient has spurting bleeding from the forearm and gurgling respirations. In what order should you act?
choices: Suction the airway, then control the bleeding
Control the bleeding with a tourniquet, then manage the airway
Apply oxygen, then take vitals, then control bleeding
Immobilize the spine before anything else
quiz.why: Massive external hemorrhage precedes airway in the XABC sequence because arterial bleeding empties the vascular space in minutes. The airway is addressed immediately afterward, and spinal care comes later.

quiz.q: A question stem ends with 'Which of the following should you do NEXT?' after describing that you have opened the airway and confirmed adequate breathing. What is being asked?
choices: To repeat the airway assessment
To choose the action that follows breathing in the priority sequence
To select the most advanced intervention available
To choose whatever your local protocol lists first
quiz.why: 'Next' assumes the preceding steps are complete and asks what follows, which here is circulation. Repeating a completed step and answering from local protocol are both classic ways to lose an easy item.

quiz.q: During a spinal immobilization skill station, a candidate secures the head to the board before securing the torso. What is the result?
choices: A minor point deduction
No effect if the final result is secure
A critical criteria failure for the station
The station is restarted from the beginning
quiz.why: Securing the head first allows the torso to shift beneath it, which moves the cervical spine. Torso-before-head is a listed critical criterion and violating it fails the station regardless of the rest.

quiz.q: You have completed 65 questions on the cognitive exam and feel that most were guesses. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: You are almost certainly failing and should slow down drastically
You should answer a few deliberately wrong to make the questions easier
The test has malfunctioned
This is the expected experience, because the algorithm targets the edge of your ability
quiz.why: An adaptive test deliberately serves items you have roughly a 50-50 chance on, so uncertainty is the normal feel of passing. Deliberately missing items lowers your ability estimate toward the failing side.

scenarios.title: Question dissection: airway, breathing and the word FIRST
scenarios.intro: Five exam-style items, one per step. For each, read the stem, find the cue word, predict your answer before looking at the choices, then pick. The feedback explains not just the medicine but why the National Registry wrote the item this way and what the distractors were designed to catch.

steps.prompt: **Item 1.** You respond to a 47-year-old male found unresponsive on a bathroom floor. He has snoring respirations at about 8 per minute and a weak radial pulse. Which of the following should you do FIRST?

choices.text: Open the airway with a head-tilt chin-lift
choices.feedback: Correct. The cue word is FIRST, and snoring is the tongue blocking the airway. Positioning costs one second and requires no equipment. Everything else in this item depends on a patent airway existing.

choices.text: Begin assisted ventilations with a bag-valve mask
choices.feedback: This patient does need ventilation at 8 per minute, which makes it a very tempting distractor. But bagging through an obstructed airway pushes air into the stomach. Open first, then ventilate — that is the whole point of the word FIRST.

choices.text: Apply a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min
choices.feedback: Wrong on two counts. A mask does nothing through a blocked airway, and a rate of 8 with inadequate depth calls for assisted ventilation rather than passive oxygen. This is the 'everyone gets oxygen' reflex the exam hunts for.

choices.text: Obtain a set of baseline vital signs
choices.feedback: Vitals belong after the primary survey. Any answer that gathers data while a life threat is untreated is wrong when the stem says FIRST.

steps.prompt: **Item 2.** You have opened the airway of the same patient and inserted an oropharyngeal airway without resistance. His respirations remain about 8 per minute and shallow. Which of the following should you do NEXT?

choices.text: Apply a nasal cannula at 4 L/min
choices.feedback: No. A cannula only supplements a patient who is moving adequate air. At 8 shallow breaths, the problem is volume of air moved, and a cannula does not move air.

choices.text: Ventilate with a bag-valve mask connected to oxygen at 15 L/min
choices.feedback: Correct. The cue word is NEXT, meaning the airway step is done, so you move to breathing. A rate of 8 with shallow depth is inadequate ventilation, and the treatment for inadequate ventilation is always to ventilate.

choices.text: Check a blood glucose level
choices.feedback: It is a reasonable thing to do eventually for an unresponsive patient, but it belongs after breathing is managed. The exam consistently ranks an untreated ventilation problem above any diagnostic step.

choices.text: Perform a rapid head-to-toe assessment
choices.feedback: Secondary assessment comes after the primary survey is complete and its problems are corrected. Moving on with inadequate ventilation is the error this distractor tests for.

steps.prompt: **Item 3.** A 68-year-old with a history of COPD is short of breath and speaking in short sentences. Room-air saturation is `86%`. He is alert with adequate chest rise. Which is the MOST APPROPRIATE oxygen therapy?

choices.text: Withhold oxygen to preserve his hypoxic drive
choices.feedback: This is outdated teaching that persists in study groups and it is wrong. Hypoxia kills faster than any theoretical loss of respiratory drive, and 86 percent is real hypoxia that must be treated.

choices.text: Nonrebreather at 15 L/min until the saturation reaches 100%
choices.feedback: Over-treatment. The COPD target is 88 to 92 percent; driving a COPD patient to 100 percent worsens ventilation-perfusion matching and can blunt drive. The word MOST APPROPRIATE means several choices give oxygen and only one gives the right dose.

choices.text: Titrate oxygen to a saturation of 88 to 92%
choices.feedback: Correct. He is hypoxic and gets oxygen, but to the COPD target, not to 100 percent. Oxygen is a drug with a dose, and MOST APPROPRIATE is asking you to name the dose.

choices.text: Begin bag-valve-mask ventilation
choices.feedback: He is alert with adequate chest rise, so he is ventilating — he is just hypoxic. Bagging an alert patient who is moving air is an unnecessary and harmful intervention.

steps.prompt: **Item 4.** A 3-year-old with a two-day history of a barking cough is sitting on her mother's lap with mild retractions and stridor only when she cries. She is alert, pink and consolable. Which action is MOST APPROPRIATE?

choices.text: Examine the throat with a tongue blade to rule out epiglottitis
choices.feedback: Never, in any child with stridor. If the diagnosis were epiglottitis, that maneuver can cause complete obstruction. When a choice can kill the patient if you guessed wrong about the diagnosis, it is not the answer.

choices.text: Keep her on her mother's lap, provide blow-by oxygen, minimize agitation, and transport
choices.feedback: Correct. Croup obstruction worsens with agitation, so calm is a treatment. MOST APPROPRIATE here is testing whether you know that doing less, gently, beats doing more.

choices.text: Place a pediatric nonrebreather tightly on her face and lay her supine
choices.feedback: Both halves are wrong. Forcing a mask causes screaming and worsens upper-airway obstruction, and supine positioning makes it worse still. Let the child pick the position.

choices.text: Insert a nasopharyngeal airway to bypass the swelling
choices.feedback: An NPA does not reach subglottic swelling, and inserting it in an awake child causes agitation and bleeding. It is a plausible-sounding intervention that treats the wrong level of the airway.

steps.prompt: **Item 5.** An unresponsive 30-year-old has pinpoint pupils, respirations of 4 per minute, and a saturation of `74%`. Your unit carries intranasal naloxone. Which of the following should you do FIRST?

choices.text: Administer 4 mg intranasal naloxone
choices.feedback: The most seductive distractor on the exam. Naloxone is absolutely indicated, but it takes 2 to 5 minutes to work and he is at 74 percent right now. The word FIRST separates the correct drug from the correct sequence.

choices.text: Open the airway and begin ventilating with a bag-valve mask
choices.feedback: Correct. Opioid patients die of hypoxia, not of unconsciousness. Ventilation fixes the lethal problem immediately, and naloxone is given while ventilation continues, not instead of it.

choices.text: Begin chest compressions
choices.feedback: He has a pulse of 58 and a blood pressure. Compressions on a perfusing patient are harmful, and the stem gave you the vitals specifically so you would not choose this.

choices.text: Apply a nonrebreather at 15 L/min and monitor
choices.feedback: A mask requires the patient to move air, and at 4 breaths per minute he is not. This is the single most common airway error on the exam: giving oxygen to someone who needs ventilation.

scenarios.debrief: Five items, one skill. The cue word told you which rung of the ladder the question was standing on. FIRST means the earliest step in the sequence, which is why naloxone lost to bagging and why a nonrebreather lost to opening an airway. NEXT means the previous rung is done, so you move down the list and do not repeat yourself. MOST APPROPRIATE means more than one choice is defensible and you are being asked for the right dose, the right gentleness, or the right level. Two patterns repeat across the whole airway domain. First, a patient who is not moving adequate air needs ventilation, never a mask — the exam offers the mask every single time. Second, a choice that would be catastrophic if your diagnosis were wrong, like inspecting the throat of a stridorous child, is never the answer.

scenarios.title: Question dissection: trauma, cardiac and operations
scenarios.intro: Five more exam-style items, drawn from the domains people under-study. Same method: read the stem, find the cue word, predict your answer, then pick. The feedback names the reasoning the National Registry is testing and the specific error each distractor was built to catch.

steps.prompt: **Item 1.** A 34-year-old was ejected from a vehicle. He has spurting bright red bleeding from the left forearm and gurgling respirations. Which of the following is your PRIORITY?

choices.text: Suction the airway
choices.feedback: This would be the answer in almost every other trauma item, which is what makes it a good distractor. Arterial bleeding is the one thing that outranks the airway, because he can empty his vascular space in a couple of minutes.

choices.text: Apply a tourniquet above the wound and note the time
choices.feedback: Correct. This is the X in XABC — massive external hemorrhage precedes airway. PRIORITY means ranked by threat to life, and exsanguination is faster than the gurgling.

choices.text: Apply high-flow oxygen and obtain vital signs
choices.feedback: Oxygen does nothing for a patient who is losing the blood that carries it, and vitals during an active life threat is always wrong. This distractor catches people who study the numbers instead of the order.

choices.text: Apply full spinal immobilization before anything else
choices.feedback: The mechanism justifies spinal precautions, but not before hemorrhage and airway. Any choice that immobilizes a bleeding, gurgling patient first is testing whether you rank mechanism above life threats.

steps.prompt: **Item 2.** A 59-year-old woman is nauseated, sweaty, and extremely fatigued with mild discomfort between her shoulder blades. She denies chest pain. She is diabetic. Which condition should you SUSPECT?

choices.text: Acute coronary syndrome presenting atypically
choices.feedback: Correct. The cue is SUSPECT, which asks for pattern recognition, not treatment. Women, diabetics and older adults frequently have infarctions without chest pain, showing nausea, fatigue, dyspnea or back and jaw discomfort instead.

choices.text: Anxiety attack
choices.feedback: The classic wrong call that gets women with heart attacks sent home. Nothing in the stem supports anxiety, and the diabetic history plus diaphoresis points the other way.

choices.text: Musculoskeletal back strain
choices.feedback: Back strain does not produce diaphoresis, nausea and profound fatigue together. The exam includes an innocent-sounding option in every atypical-presentation item to see if you will take it.

choices.text: Hypoglycemia, because she is diabetic
choices.feedback: Worth checking a glucose, and diaphoresis does overlap. But fatigue with interscapular discomfort in a diabetic is a cardiac pattern, and hypoglycemia would not explain it alone.

steps.prompt: **Item 3.** A 66-year-old with chest pain has taken two of his own nitroglycerin tablets before your arrival. He rates his pain 7 out of 10. He has no PDE-5 inhibitor use and no allergies. His BP is now `92/58`. What is the MOST APPROPRIATE action?

choices.text: Assist with a third nitroglycerin dose since the maximum is three
choices.feedback: The dose count is a trap. The blood pressure gate is checked before every single dose, and 92 systolic is below the usual threshold of 100. Counting doses instead of checking pressure is exactly the error being tested.

choices.text: Withhold nitroglycerin, give aspirin if not already taken, position supine, and transport
choices.feedback: Correct. Nitroglycerin is out on blood pressure, but aspirin is unaffected and has a mortality benefit. MOST APPROPRIATE wants the full correct package, not just the one thing you withhold.

choices.text: Withhold both nitroglycerin and aspirin until the pressure improves
choices.feedback: Half right. Nitroglycerin is correctly withheld, but nothing about a systolic of 92 contraindicates aspirin, and withholding it removes the intervention most likely to save him.

choices.text: Give nitroglycerin but have him sit upright to reduce side effects
choices.feedback: Sitting upright makes hypotension worse, not better, and the contraindication stands regardless of position. A distractor that pairs a forbidden action with a plausible-sounding modification is a common design.

steps.prompt: **Item 4.** A bus crash has produced 14 patients. You are the first arriving unit. A patient sitting up is breathing 34 times per minute with a strong radial pulse and follows commands. Using START triage, what is the correct category?

choices.text: Delayed (yellow), since the pulse and mental status are normal
choices.feedback: A very common miss. START stops at the first abnormal finding, and the respiratory rate was already abnormal before you ever got to pulse and mental status.

choices.text: Minor (green), since he is sitting up
choices.feedback: Sitting up is not the green criterion — walking is. Green is for the ambulatory who can move themselves to a collection area, and this patient has a respiratory rate of 34.

choices.text: Immediate (red), because the respiratory rate is over 30
choices.feedback: Correct. In START, a rate over 30 alone tags the patient immediate. The algorithm is deliberately blunt so that it runs fast, and you stop evaluating once a criterion is met.

choices.text: Expectant (black), because resources are limited
choices.feedback: Expectant applies only to a patient not breathing after the airway is opened. Resource scarcity never changes the category of a breathing patient who follows commands.

steps.prompt: **Item 5.** An alert, oriented 52-year-old with chest pain, a normal blood pressure, and a clear understanding of her situation states she will not go to the hospital. Which of the following is the MOST APPROPRIATE action?

choices.text: Transport her under implied consent because her condition is potentially life-threatening
choices.feedback: Implied consent applies only to patients who cannot consent for themselves. Transporting a competent adult against her will is false imprisonment, no matter how sick she might be.

choices.text: Have her sign the refusal form and clear the call
choices.feedback: Incomplete. A signature is not the refusal — the informed risk discussion is. A form signed without documenting what she was told and that she understood will not stand up to review.

choices.text: Explain the specific risks in plain language, confirm she understands them, encourage transport, document the discussion, and obtain a witness
choices.feedback: Correct. A valid refusal requires capacity plus genuine informed understanding, documented in detail with a witness. MOST APPROPRIATE is asking for the complete process, not one step of it.

choices.text: Ask her husband to sign the refusal on her behalf
choices.feedback: A competent adult speaks for herself. A family member cannot consent or refuse for a patient who has decision-making capacity, and doing so invalidates the documentation.

scenarios.debrief: The reasoning repeats across every domain. PRIORITY means ranked by how fast the problem kills, which is why arterial bleeding beat a gurgling airway. SUSPECT means pattern recognition only, so the answer is a diagnosis rather than an action, and atypical cardiac presentations in women, diabetics and older adults are one of the exam's favorite patterns. MOST APPROPRIATE means the complete correct package — withhold the one drug, give the other, position, transport — and the distractors are built from partial answers that get one piece right. Two structural habits are worth keeping. Distractors that pair a forbidden action with a reassuring modification, like nitroglycerin plus sitting upright, are always wrong. And in operations and legal items, the answer is nearly always the conservative, fully documented, by-the-book action, because those items are testing whether you protect the patient's rights and everyone's safety rather than whether you know medicine.
